item.title: What does “one in three cannot read” measure?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
On November 25, CTV News reported on two papers from the Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy [3]. The first is titled “One in Three 9-Year-Old Canadians Cannot Read” [1]. The second says that, depending on the province, between 20 and 56 percent of students cannot read by Grade 4 [2].

I downloaded the public data behind the provincial figures for British Columbia, Manitoba, and Ontario, and worked through them. The concern in the reports is a fair one. A large share of young students are below their province’s standard, and in Manitoba and Ontario the share grew after the pandemic. The headline numbers, however, do not measure one thing. They come from different tests, different years, and different denominators, and the range from 20 to 56 says more about those differences than about reading.

Seven provinces, seven yardsticks

The first report’s Figure 2 places seven provinces side by side under the label “most recent year.” The report notes that Grade 3 and Grade 4 results “are not perfectly comparable” [1]. The differences go further than the grade.

Alberta’s 20% is the share below the Intermediate benchmark. On the same test, about 5% of Alberta students were below the Low benchmark [10]. “Cannot read” fits neither number well, and it fits the first one poorly.

Manitoba’s assessment is the furthest from the others. It is classroom-based, it is done early in the school year, and a student counts as meeting expectations only if the teacher judges that all three sub-competencies are met [5]. A student who meets two of three is counted with those who meet none. That rule produces a low percentage by construction. It does not make Manitoba’s result unimportant, and I return to it below.

Ontario’s figure is seven years old. The Education Quality and Accountability Office (EQAO) has published four rounds of results since then. In 2025–26, 75% of fully participating Grade 3 students met the reading standard [6]. A representative of Dyslexia Canada made the same point in the CTV story [3].

In British Columbia, the answer depends on who wrote the test

The report does not give a year for BC’s 30%. The open data reproduce it: 30.2% of Grade 4 students in public schools were not on track in literacy in 2025/26 [4]. With independent schools included, the figure is 27.3%.

Those percentages are shares of the students who wrote. In BC that matters, because many students do not write the Foundation Skills Assessment, and the number who do has changed.

Between 2021/22 and 2024/25, the published not-on-track share rose from 22% to 34%. Over the same years, participation rose from 73% to 85%. Counted as a share of all Grade 4 students expected to write, the on-track group stayed between 57% and 61% in every year from 2017/18 to 2025/26.

I cannot tell from these files how much of the rise is a decline in reading and how much is the arrival of students who would not have written in earlier years. The published rate alone cannot separate the two. A year-to-year comparison of that rate, without the participation figure beside it, is not safe.

Ontario changed its denominator in 2022

Before the pandemic, EQAO reported the share of all Grade 3 students who met the standard. Since 2021–22, it reports the share of fully participating students [8]. EQAO restated its 2018–19 result on the new basis when it made the change [9]. I computed the 2021–22 result on the old basis from EQAO’s published counts [6].

A reader who compares the 74% published in 2019 with the 73% published in 2022 would conclude that almost nothing happened. Both like-for-like comparisons show a drop.

The drop was not even. I followed about 2,600 English-language schools that have results before and after. On the all-students basis, Grade 3 reading fell by about 5 points in the third of schools with the fewest low-income families and by about 9 points in the third with the most [6, 7]. By 2024–25 the gap from the pre-pandemic level had narrowed to about 3 and 6 points.

One caution applies to all of these comparisons. Ontario moved from a paper test to an online adaptive test between 2019 and 2022. The change in the numbers is the pandemic and the change of test together.

Manitoba has the cleanest record of the pandemic

Manitoba used one assessment and one reporting rule from Fall 2015 to Fall 2025, with no assessment in Fall 2020 [5]. No other province I examined offers that.

The provincial share was 49.3% in Fall 2019 and 44.9% in Fall 2021. It was 45.3% in Fall 2025. Against the trend of the five years before the pandemic, the drop is about 5 points, and the provincial figure has not recovered.

Among Indigenous students the share fell from 29.9% to 23.0%, and it has since risen to 28.2%. Among non-Indigenous students it fell from 54.2% to 50.6%, and it was 49.7% in Fall 2025.

This is a teacher’s judgment against a rubric. A shift in the series could be a shift in how teachers apply the rubric. I have no evidence that this happened, and the size and timing of the drop are what the pandemic would produce.

One year of results does not rank schools

The reports discuss provinces, but the same data are used to compare schools and districts, so I checked how dependable a single year is.

In Ontario, a school’s Grade 3 reading percentage in one year has a reliability of about 0.62 for ranking schools across the province. An average over three years reaches about 0.83. The median school has 33 students in Grade 3, and a percentage based on 33 students moves several points from year to year when nothing about the school has changed.

In BC, about four in five year-to-year changes in a school’s mean score are within the range that the sampling of students alone would produce.

What this does not show

It does not show that literacy is fine. In Ontario, 25% to 30% of Grade 3 students do not meet the provincial reading standard, depending on the denominator. In Manitoba, more than half of Grade 3 students do not meet all three expectations early in the year. These are large numbers on any reading.

It does not test the reports’ argument about how reading should be taught. Nothing here compares structured literacy with other approaches. The reforms are recent, and the students taught under them have not yet reached the tests that would show an effect.

It does not measure a pandemic effect in BC. In 2020/21, the first sitting after the closures, participation fell to 67% and the rate among writers rose. The test then changed. The BC data cannot settle the question in either direction.

It does not check the second report’s statement that Grade 10 students are two to three years behind their peers of 25 years ago. The source given for that statement is another paper by the same authors, listed as forthcoming [2].

What would settle it

Three things would help.

  1. Every province could publish counts alongside percentages: students enrolled, students who wrote, and students who met the standard. Ontario does this now. BC masks most of these counts at the school level.
  2. A common yardstick exists. Students in several provinces wrote the PIRLS Grade 4 reading assessment in spring 2026, and the international results are due in December 2027. Those students are the first to be assessed internationally after the recent curriculum changes.
  3. Reports that compare provinces could state, for each number, the test, the year, and the denominator.

The international assessments are the subject of a second post. The R scripts behind every number in this post are available on request. If you find an error, please tell me.

References

  1. Livingstone D, Hunt D, Tran P. One in Three 9-Year-Old Canadians Cannot Read. Reality Check. Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy, November 13, 2026.
  2. Livingstone D, Hunt D, Tran P. Why Literacy Is at an All-Time Low—and What to Do About It. Reality Check. Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy, November 18, 2026.
  3. Dabu C. Education think tank calls for change in teaching literacy in Canada. CTV News, November 25, 2026.
  4. BC Ministry of Education and Child Care. BC Schools: Foundation Skills Assessment. BC Data Catalogue, extracts for 2007/08 to 2025/26.
  5. Manitoba Education and Early Childhood Learning. K–12 Education Data Dashboard: Grade 3 and 4 Assessment, and Grade 3 assessment results.
  6. Education Quality and Accountability Office. Open data: Grade 3 and Grade 6 achievement results, 2021–22 to 2025–26.
  7. Ontario Ministry of Education. School information and student demographics, 2017–18 to 2024–25.
  8. Education Quality and Accountability Office. Highlights of the Provincial Results: Grade 3, 2021–2022.
  9. Education Quality and Accountability Office. 2021–2022 provincial results. News release, 2022.
  10. IEA TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center. PIRLS 2021 International Benchmarks.

item.title: Reading at 15 fell twice, and the second fall was different
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
In an earlier post I looked at the provincial figures behind the claim that one in three 9-year-old Canadians cannot read, and I said I would write again about the international tests. This post does that. It uses the public student files from PISA, the OECD’s assessment of 15-year-olds, for 2018, 2022, and 2025 [1], and the PIRLS Grade 4 files for 2016 and 2021 [3].

My estimates reproduce the published ones. For Canada in 2022 I obtain a reading mean of 507 with a standard error of 2.0, and for Alberta on PIRLS 2021 a mean of 539 with a standard error of 3.6. Both match the official reports [2, 3].

The decline did not stop in 2022

The mean fell 13 points from 2018 to 2022 and a further 17 points from 2022 to 2025. Both changes are several times their standard errors, with the link error between cycles included.

The 2022 result was widely read as the cost of the pandemic. If school closures were the whole story, the three years after 2022 should show a pause or a partial recovery. They show a second drop at least as large as the first.

The two drops are not the same

From 2018 to 2022, the weakest readers lost the most. The score at the 10th percentile fell 22 points, and the score at the 90th percentile fell 3, a change that is within sampling error. That pattern is what an interruption of schooling would produce if stronger students were better able to keep learning without it.

From 2022 to 2025, the loss was about the same everywhere: 15 to 21 points at every percentile I examined. Strong readers, who had held their ground through the pandemic years, fell as far as weak ones.

I do not know what caused the second drop. The data rule out some explanations, which I take up below, and they do not identify one.

The provinces fell at different times

Every province scored lower in 2025 than in 2018 [2]. The timing differs.

  • Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and Saskatchewan took most of their decline by 2022 and changed little afterward.
  • Alberta, British Columbia, and Prince Edward Island changed little by 2022 and fell afterward. Alberta fell 26 points between 2022 and 2025.
  • Quebec, Ontario, and New Brunswick fell in both periods. Manitoba fell by 8 and 9 points, the smallest total decline along with Saskatchewan’s.

The provincial figures for 2025 are CMEC’s. The public file for 2025 does not identify provinces within Canada, so I could not recompute them.

Three explanations the data do not support

A change in who is in the classroom. I reweighted the 2025 sample so that the shares of non-immigrant, second-generation, and first-generation students match those of 2018. The 2025 mean moves from 490 to 492. Immigration does not explain a 30-point decline.

A change in who wrote the test. About 77% of sampled students took part in both 2022 and 2025, and Statistics Canada found that the students who took part had higher school marks than those who did not [2]. That biases each year’s score upward. It biases the change only if the bias itself changed. For the 17-point drop to be an artefact, the gap between participants and non-participants would have had to shrink by about 75 points in three years, with participation unchanged. The OECD’s own review reached the same view and called the effect on the 2022 to 2025 comparison negligible [2].

The pandemic alone. The cohort tested in 2025 was in Grade 4 or 5 when schools closed in 2020, so lasting harm from the closures is possible. A closure effect, however, would be expected to look like the first drop and fall hardest on weak readers. The second drop does not look like that.

In Grade 4, where a comparison exists, there is no drop

Quebec is the only province with its own PIRLS sample in both 2016 and 2021. Its Grade 4 mean was 547 in 2016 and 551 in 2021, a difference within sampling error. The share of students below the Low benchmark was 1.6% and 1.2%.

In 2021, the share below the Low benchmark was 5.0% in Alberta, 5.7% in British Columbia, and 7.5% in Newfoundland and Labrador. The share below the Intermediate benchmark, which is the figure the Aristotle Foundation report used for Alberta [4], was 20%, 21%, and 26%.

One province and one pair of years is thin evidence. It is still worth setting beside the 15-year-old results: the largest measured declines are in adolescence, and the public debate is about how reading is taught in Grades 1 to 3.

What this does not show

It does not show why scores fell after 2022. The candidates people raise, among them phones, attendance, and the long tail of the closures, are not tested here.

It does not show that the 2025 numbers are exact. Canada did not meet the PISA standard for student participation in 2022 or 2025, and seven provinces carry a caution flag in 2025 [2]. The levels are probably somewhat too high in both years. The change between them is on firmer ground than either level.

It does not bear on the early-reading reforms. A student who started Grade 1 under Alberta’s new curriculum in 2022 will be 15 in about 2031.

What would settle it

The 2025 public file has no province codes for Canada. With them, the percentile analysis above could be done province by province, and one could see whether Alberta’s late drop looks like Newfoundland’s early one. CMEC holds those codes.

PIRLS 2026 was written last spring. Its results, due in December 2027, will give Grade 4 figures that can be set against 2021 for more provinces than Quebec.

The R scripts behind these numbers are available on request. If you find an error, please tell me.

References

  1. OECD. PISA database: student questionnaire data files, 2018, 2022, and 2025.
  2. Elez V, et al. Measuring Up: Canadian Results of the OECD PISA 2025 Study. Council of Ministers of Education, Canada, 2026. Tables B.3.21c and B.3.21d, and Appendix A.
  3. IEA TIMSS & PIRLS International Study Center. PIRLS 2021 International Database and PIRLS 2016 International Database.
  4. Livingstone D, Hunt D, Tran P. One in Three 9-Year-Old Canadians Cannot Read. Aristotle Foundation for Public Policy, November 13, 2026.

item.title: What does a count of 29,000 waiting-list deaths tell us?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
In November 2026 SecondStreet.org reported 29,468 cases in 2025-26 in which a surgery, procedure, diagnostic scan, or specialist appointment was cancelled because the patient had died [1]. CTV News carried it as at least 29,000 Canadians who died while waiting [2]. Its video report added that deaths among people waiting for surgery had risen 17.5% in a year [3].

Waits for care in Canada are long, and some people die because care came too late. That deserves attention. The question I ask here is narrower: what can this count support? I went through the freedom-of-information responses that SecondStreet posted with its report, and I set the counts beside published waiting-list sizes and Statistics Canada life tables. The full report runs to 35 pages [10]. It is preliminary and has not been peer reviewed. This post gives the main findings.

The count has no ages

None of the 34 documents gives the age of a single patient. The requests did not ask for it.

Age matters because people on surgical and imaging lists are mostly older, and older people die at known rates whether or not they are waiting. In British Columbia in 2024, the chance of dying within a year was 0.8% at age 65, 2.0% at age 75, and 6.1% at age 85 [6]. Of the people who had a knee replacement in BC, 72% were 65 or older and 29% were 75 or older [7]. A count of deaths among people on a list therefore needs a benchmark: the number of deaths expected in a group of the same size and age over the same period. Nobody has made that comparison for this count, because the ages are missing.

The count is also a count of cancelled bookings, and one person can hold several. Vancouver Coastal Health’s imaging table has 1.23 bookings per patient, and one Quebec health body lists 532 waits for 459 patients. Of the 29,468 cases, 5,931 are surgeries and procedures. The other 23,537 are scans and requests to see a specialist.

Death rates on surgical lists, read as ages

One comparison needs no ages. Divide the deaths recorded on a surgical list by the number of people waiting through the year, and the result is a death rate. A life table then gives the age at which the general population dies at that rate.

The five regional health authorities in BC recorded 900 deaths in 2025-26 on lists that averaged about 91,500 cases through the year [5]. That is 0.98 deaths per 100 person-years of waiting, the rate at which British Columbians aged 67 die. The table gives the same calculation wherever a list size is published.

Deaths recorded on surgical waiting lists in 2025-26. Rate is deaths per 100 person-years on the list. Age is the age at which the general population of that province dies at that rate. Nova Scotia’s count is a range because 41 of its rows are withheld as fewer than five. Manitoba and Prince Edward Island publish no list size. The list sizes are in the report [10], and those for the Quebec regions are from the provincial waiting-list file [9].
Province or region Deaths Rate Age
British Columbia 900 0.98 67
Alberta 878 1.07 67
Saskatchewan 317 1.04 65
Ontario 1,291 0.60 61
New Brunswick 91 0.43 54
Nova Scotia 127 to 250 0.79 to 1.56 62 to 69
Quebec: Estrie 162 1.57 71
Quebec: Outaouais 78 1.20 68
Quebec: Abitibi-Témiscamingue 37 1.47 70

Alberta is the most informative row. It is the one province that finds these deaths by linking its waiting list to dates of death, and it counts people, not bookings. Its rate is the general-population rate at age 67, the same age as in BC.

The low rates need a caution. New Brunswick’s is the rate of the general population at age 54, and that more likely means its registry misses deaths than that its patients are that young.

Where ages are known, fewer deaths were recorded than age alone predicts

Knee replacement is the one list for which I have real ages, because CIHI publishes them [7]. Given those ages, the BC life table predicts 131 to 150 deaths in a year among the people waiting for a knee replacement in four BC health authorities. Those authorities recorded 56.

Two things could produce that gap, and the counts cannot separate them. People accepted for a knee replacement are healthier than others of their age. Booking offices also do not learn of every death. The result holds unless the people waiting are nine to ten years younger than the people who had the operation.

For surgery as a whole I had to assume the ages, and the comparison is sensitive to what I assume, so I put little weight on it.

The provinces are not counting the same thing

The recorded rates in the table differ nearly fourfold. The responses show why they would.

Cataract surgery. Patients waiting for cataract surgery are 63% of New Brunswick’s count and 26% to 37% of the count in six other provinces. Manitoba’s main response has no cataract cases at all.

One number in Quebec. Half of Quebec’s surgical total, 967 of 1,879, is a single figure from the Laurentides region for “surgical intervention or medical act.” Set against that region’s surgical list, it would be 11 deaths per 100 person-years, the rate at which the general population dies at age 88.

Scans ordered near the end of life. Ontario released 9,085 CT and MRI bookings that were cancelled because the patient died. Among the 754 with a two-day target, 46% were cancelled within a day of the order. Those are urgent scans, most likely for very sick patients, and they are in the count beside people who waited for months. Most of the Ontario bookings did wait: 82% had been open longer than their target when they were cancelled.

The 17.5% rise comes from one health region

SecondStreet’s brief says that, among health bodies that provided data in both years, surgical waitlist deaths rose 17.5% [1]. The figure can be reproduced from the tables in its 2025 and 2026 briefs [1, 4]. Twenty-two health bodies have a surgical count in both tables, with 4,300 cases in 2024-25 and 5,053 in 2025-26.

Surgical cases cancelled because the patient died, in the health bodies behind the 17.5% figure.
Health bodies 2024‑25 2025‑26 Change
All 22 with a surgical count in both years 4,300 5,053 +17.5%
Laurentides, Quebec 134 967 +622%
The other 21 4,166 4,086 −1.9%
The 12 outside Quebec 3,280 3,174 −3.2%

The count for Laurentides rose by 833. The net rise across all 22 bodies is 753. Without Laurentides, the count fell.

The Laurentides figure for 2025-26 is the “surgical intervention or medical act” number described above, and the response says it includes endoscopy. The region’s figure for 2024-25 gives 1.3 deaths per 100 person-years, in line with other regions of Quebec. Its surgical list was 15% smaller in the second year. A sevenfold rise in deaths on a shrinking list is not credible as a change in mortality. The likelier explanation is that the two responses cover different sets of patients, and only the health body can confirm that.

The other bodies do not share a trend either. Across the 22, counts rose in 10 and fell in 12. Ontario Health says of its own imaging count that the change from year to year is driven mainly by how hospitals record cancelled entries. In BC, where the list size is known in both years, the rate went from 0.92 deaths per 100 person-years to 0.98, on a list of the same size. That is the general-population rate at age 66, and then at age 67.

The headline number itself rose from 23,746 to 29,468. Almost all of that rise is a change in what was reported.

Where the rise from 23,746 to 29,468 comes from. The new figures are Alberta’s surgical count and specialist and diagnostic counts from five Quebec health bodies.
Source of the change in the headline number Cases
Figures reported in both years +295
Figures new in 2025-26 +8,560
Figures from 2024-25 that dropped out −3,133
Change in the total +5,722

What this does not show

None of this shows that waiting is harmless. The counts cannot say how many of these deaths the wait caused, and that is true in both directions. Some registries appear to miss deaths, so the number of people who died while waiting could be higher than recorded. A study of Ontario patients waiting for bypass surgery found that they died at about three times the rate of the general population of the same age [8]. That study could say so because it had each patient’s age and time on the list.

SecondStreet’s brief makes a related point: no government analysed how many of these cases involved a delay that contributed to the death [1]. It cites the one review I know of, by Nova Scotia for 2022-23, in which 50 of 532 waiting-list deaths involved procedures where delay might reasonably have played a part.

My own estimate of the ages, from a model that weights each waiting list by life-table mortality, is that 60% to 74% of the surgical-list deaths were of people aged 75 and over. It rests largely on assumed ages and is the least secure result in the report.

I take no position here on how health care should be delivered or paid for. The argument is about what one count can show.

What would settle it

A province can answer the question with one table: the number of people who died while on a surgical or imaging list, by age group, procedure, and priority, found by linking the list to death registrations, and set beside the number expected from the life table. Alberta already does the linkage.

On November 25 I asked the five BC regional health authorities for their counts by age group. I will write again when the answers arrive.

SecondStreet posted every response it received, and that is what made this check possible. If you find an error in the report, please tell me.

References

  1. Craig C. Died on a Waiting List, 2026 Edition. Policy brief. SecondStreet.org, November 2026. Brief (PDF). Freedom-of-information responses.
  2. Wright H. At least 29,000 Canadians died over last year while waiting for medical procedure, scan or specialist. CTV News, November 2026.
  3. CTV News. At least 29,000 Canadians died over last year while waiting for medical procedure. Video, November 2026.
  4. Craig C. Died on a Waiting List, 2025 Edition. Policy brief. SecondStreet.org, November 2025.
  5. BC Ministry of Health. BC Surgical Wait Times, annual file, 2009/10 to 2025/26.
  6. Statistics Canada. Table 13-10-0837-01. Life expectancy and other elements of the complete life table.
  7. Canadian Institute for Health Information. Hip and Knee Replacements in Canada: CJRR Annual Report, 2024–2025.
  8. Naylor CD, Szalai JP, Katic M. Benchmarking the vital risk of waiting for coronary artery bypass surgery in Ontario. CMAJ 2000;162(6):775–779.
  9. Ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux. Chirurgies: portrait de la liste d’attente. Données Québec.
  10. Karunanayaka RC. Deaths on waiting lists in British Columbia, 2025–26: what the published counts show without patient ages. Interim report, third version, November 25, 2026. It lists the sources for the other provinces’ list sizes.

item.title: Is a striker who beats his xG a good finisher?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Expected goals, or xG, gives every shot a probability of becoming a goal, based on where it was taken from and how. Add up those probabilities over a season and you get the number of goals an average finisher would have scored from the same chances. A striker who scores more than that number is said to be finishing well. One who scores fewer is said to be wasteful.

It is a reasonable idea, and the number is now quoted on every broadcast. The question a statistician asks is how much of the gap between goals and xG could happen by chance.

One season of shots

Take a striker who has 80 shots in a season, each worth about 0.12 expected goals. His xG for the season is 9.6.

Even if he is exactly an average finisher, he will not score exactly 9.6 goals. Each shot either goes in or it does not, and the number of goals varies from season to season around 9.6. For shots like these, the standard deviation of that variation is about 2.9 goals.

So an average finisher will often finish a season 3 goals above his xG, or 3 below, by luck alone. A gap of that size, which commentators treat as a verdict on a player’s finishing, is about one standard deviation of chance.

How long does it take to see real skill?

Suppose the striker really is better than average, and converts his chances at a rate 10% higher than xG expects: 0.132 per shot instead of 0.12. Over a season of 80 shots, that skill is worth about one extra goal. The chance variation is close to three goals.

For the skill to stand out clearly, at about two standard deviations of chance, the arithmetic says he needs roughly 2,900 shots. At 80 shots a season, that is more than 35 seasons, which is longer than any career.

The numbers are illustrative, and real shots differ in quality, which changes the details. The conclusion is hard to escape: over the seasons a player actually plays, a gap between goals and xG is mostly noise, unless the gap is very large.

What this does and does not mean

It does not mean finishing skill is a myth. Some players almost certainly finish better than others. It means a single season, or even a few seasons, of goals minus xG is too little data to tell who they are.

It also does not mean xG is a poor tool. Its strength is that it is built from many shots across many players, which makes it far more stable than goals. The trouble starts when a team-level or league-level tool is used to judge one player over one season.

Even xG needs time

The arithmetic above is about goals minus xG. A related question is how many matches a player’s xG itself needs before it can rank players dependably. I have been studying this with event data from five recent men’s international tournaments.

It takes more than one tournament. Only about one-eighth of the match-to-match variation in a player’s xG reflects stable ability. The rest comes from the match, the opponent, and the circumstances. At that level, ranking attacking players dependably takes roughly 27 matches, or about three tournament cycles. Spreading observations across tournaments helps more than adding matches within one.

One result surprised me. If you count only the matches in which a player took a shot, defenders look like the most consistent xG producers. Count every match they played, including the many with no shots, and they become the least consistent, while forwards become the most. Which matches you include can reverse the answer, and the same risk applies to any statistic a player records only now and then.

The general lesson

This is the same question I have written about for batting averages and counts in general: how many observations does a number need before it describes the player rather than the luck? For a rare event like a goal, the answer is usually far more than a season provides.

How many games, shots, or sessions a performance measure needs before it can be trusted is a question I help sports organizations answer. See work with sports organizations.

item.title: What a GPS vest can tell a soccer coach, and what it cannot
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Many soccer teams, including university and academy sides, now put a GPS vest on every player at training and in matches. After each session the coach gets a table: total distance, distance at high speed, number of sprints, and top speed, for every player.

The table looks precise. The question is which of its numbers describe the player and which describe the day.

Three sources of variation

Any number from a vest moves for three reasons.

  1. The player. Some players really are faster, or cover more ground, than others. This is what the coach wants to know.
  2. The session. A small-sided game, a tactical walk-through, a match against a strong opponent, and a recovery day all produce different numbers for everyone.
  3. Everything else. A player who felt flat that day, a tight hamstring, the position he was asked to play, and the error in the device itself.

The useful question is how large the first source is compared with the other two, and that depends on the measure.

Some measures settle quickly

Top speed is the clearest case. A player’s fastest sprint changes little from week to week, and the differences between players are large. A handful of sessions that include a genuine sprint is usually enough to rank a squad with confidence. The catch is that the session has to give the player a reason to sprint. A recovery day tells you nothing about top speed.

Some measures need many sessions

Total distance is mostly about the session, not the player. Everyone covers more ground in a full match than in a set-piece session, and players covering a similar role cover similar distances. To compare players on distance, compare them within the same sessions and the same positions, and average over many sessions.

Sprint counts and high-speed distance sit in between, and they are noisy for a different reason. They are counts of fairly rare events, and on any one day a player may record none. Counts like these need more sessions than an average-based measure before differences between players stand out, for the same reasons I set out in the post on counts.

Questions worth asking of your own data

  • Is the measure stable for each player? Compare each player’s numbers across similar sessions. If a player’s values swing widely, a single session says little about him.
  • Are you comparing like with like? Compare players in the same sessions and similar roles, or account for those differences in the analysis.
  • How many sessions does each comparison rest on? A ranking built on two sessions is closer to a lottery than a ranking built on ten.
  • What decision rests on the number? Monitoring a player’s load from his own history asks less of the data than choosing between two players.

These are reliability questions, and generalizability theory answers them directly: it separates the player, session, and residual variation and says how many sessions a dependable comparison needs.

If your team collects tracking data and wants to know which numbers to trust, see work with sports organizations.

item.title: You cannot test every combination, and you may not need to
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
A program with ten on/off options has configurations. With twenty options it has more than a million. Nobody tests all of them. The usual response is to test the default configuration thoroughly, try a few others that seem important, and hope.

There is a better response, and it comes from the design of experiments.

Where faults come from

A fault that appears under every configuration is found quickly. The faults that survive are the ones that need a particular setting, or a particular combination of settings, before they show themselves. The useful question is how many settings have to line up.

Kuhn, Wallace, and Gallo (2004), working at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), studied software failures from a variety of domains and asked this question. They found that the failures were caused by combinations of relatively few conditions. NIST’s summary of that series of studies is that most failures were caused by one or two settings, that failures needing three or more were progressively fewer, and that all or nearly all involved six settings or fewer.

If that pattern holds for your software, then a test suite does not have to cover every configuration. It has to cover every pair of settings, and perhaps every triple.

Covering every pair

Take three on/off options. There are eight configurations, but four tests are enough to see every pair of options at every combination of values:

Test A B C
1 off off off
2 off on on
3 on off on
4 on on off

Pick any two columns. The four combinations off/off, off/on, on/off, and on/on each appear once. A fault that needs, say, A on and C off will be exercised by test 4.

A table with this property is called a covering array. Readers of the earlier post on factorial designs will recognize this one as a half fraction of the factorial.

The saving grows quickly with the number of options. For ten on/off options, six tests cover every pair:

Test O1 O2 O3 O4 O5 O6 O7 O8 O9 O10
1 on on on on on on on on on on
2 on on on on off off off off off off
3 on off off off on on on off off off
4 off on off off on off off on on off
5 off off on off off on off on off on
6 off off off on off off on off on on

Any two columns of this table show all four combinations. Six tests stand in for 1,024 configurations, as far as pairs are concerned. The number of tests needed grows roughly with the logarithm of the number of options, so a hundred options need only a few more.

How this differs from a factorial experiment

A fractional factorial design and a covering array look alike, but they answer different questions.

A factorial experiment is built to estimate effects. Each pair of settings should appear equally often, so that the estimates are balanced and precise. That is the defining property of an orthogonal array.

A test suite is built to detect faults. A combination that triggers a fault needs to appear once. The covering array drops the requirement of equal frequency and keeps only the requirement of presence. That weaker requirement is why it can be so much smaller.

What a covering array does not do

Three limits are worth stating.

  1. A pairwise array guarantees nothing about faults that need three settings together. Arrays that cover every triple exist, and they cost more tests. How far to go depends on what a missed fault costs.
  2. The array says which configurations to run. It does not say what the correct output is. For statistical software this is the harder half of the problem, because the correct answer is often a number that is only known approximately.
  3. Real options have constraints. Some combinations are not allowed, and some options have more than two values. Both can be handled, but the construction takes more care than the tables above.

Within those limits, the argument is the same one that runs through all of experimental design. Runs are expensive, and a well chosen set of runs answers many questions at once.

Reference. Kuhn, D. R., Wallace, D. R., and Gallo, A. M. (2004). Software fault interactions and implications for software testing. IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 30(6), 418–421.

Test design for statistical and machine-learning software is part of my consulting practice.

item.title: How do you put a number on a health state?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
When a health system decides whether to pay for a new treatment, it needs to compare very different benefits. One drug reduces pain. Another restores mobility. A third extends life by a few months. To compare them, health economists use a common scale on which full health is 1 and being dead is 0. A year lived in a state valued at 0.7 counts as 0.7 of a quality-adjusted life year.

The question is where a number like 0.7 comes from.

Describing a health state

The usual starting point is a short questionnaire. The most widely used one, the EQ-5D-5L, describes health on five dimensions: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort, and anxiety or depression. Each dimension has five levels, from no problems to extreme problems.

Five dimensions with five levels each give possible health states. Each one needs a value. The full table of values for a country is called a value set.

Asking people to choose

Nobody can be asked to rate 3,125 states. One common approach is a discrete choice experiment. A respondent sees two health states side by side and says which one they would prefer to live in. Each respondent answers a modest number of these questions, and a statistical model turns the pattern of choices across many respondents into a value for every state.

The values are estimates. They depend on which people were asked and on which pairs they were shown.

Two statistical questions

Which pairs should be shown? There are 4,881,250 distinct pairs of states, and a study can show only a small fraction of them. Some pairs carry almost no information, for example when one state is better on every dimension. Choosing an efficient set of pairs is a design-of-experiments problem, and a good design gets the same precision from fewer respondents.

How dependable are the resulting values? A value set is used as if it were fixed. In practice, a different sample of respondents or a different set of pairs would have produced somewhat different values. Knowing how much they would move, and which design choices control that, is a measurement question.

Both questions matter outside the statistics. A value set feeds into decisions about which treatments are funded, so a small shift in the values can change which side of a threshold a treatment falls on.

Why I am writing about this

During my sabbatical I am working remotely on the second question with colleagues at the Centre for Health Economics Research and Evaluation (CHERE) at the University of Technology Sydney, where I hold an honorary visiting appointment. The work is in progress, and I will write about results once they are published.

Designing choice experiments and assessing the reliability of measurements are both part of my consulting practice.

item.title: What P.Stat. means for a client
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
I now hold the P.Stat. (Professional Statistician) designation from the Statistical Society of Canada. Most people who hire a statistician have never seen the letters, so here is what they mean.

What it is

P.Stat. is the professional accreditation of the Statistical Society of Canada, the national body for the discipline. It is granted to a person, after review by the Society’s accreditation committee, and it is separate from an academic degree. A degree says what someone studied. The designation says a committee of statisticians examined how that person has practised.

What the committee looks at

The application covers education in statistics, mathematics, and computing, and at least six years of professional practice. For the practice requirement I documented applied work across sport science, health research, engineering technology, and political measurement, together with teaching and published methods. Referees who know the work write to the committee directly.

Accredited statisticians also agree to the Society’s code of ethical statistical practice. In plain terms: state the limits of an analysis, do not shade a result to suit whoever is paying, and protect the data.

What it changes for you

Three things.

  • An outside check. You do not have to judge a statistician’s competence yourself. A professional body has done it.
  • A standard of conduct. If the data cannot support the conclusion you hoped for, I am bound to say so. That is the part of the job clients value most after the fact.
  • A recognized credential in reports. Grant applications, regulatory submissions, and expert reports carry more weight when the analysis is signed by an accredited professional.

It does not change how I work. It gives you a reason to expect that before we have met.

If you have a study to design or an analysis to check, get in touch.

item.title: Does the order of deliveries matter?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Every cricket commentator believes in the set-up. The fast bowler sends down a short ball that pushes the batter onto the back foot, and follows it with a full, straight one. The batter, still thinking about the last ball, is late on it. The wicket is credited to the plan as much as to the delivery.

It is a good story, and bowlers and coaches plan overs around it. The statistical question is whether it is true. Does what a bowler bowled last ball change what happens this ball, or is each delivery its own event?

Two questions inside one

A bowler makes two kinds of decision. The first is selection: how often to bowl each type of delivery to this batter in this situation. The second is sequencing: given those proportions, what order to bowl them in.

Most analysis of bowling is about selection. It asks which lengths and lines concede the fewest runs or take the most wickets. Sequencing is a different claim. It says the value of a delivery depends on the one before it. If that is so, two overs with the same six deliveries in a different order are not worth the same.

Why the data do not answer this easily

On the surface the analysis is simple. Take ball-by-ball records, group deliveries by what came before, and compare outcomes. Four problems stand in the way.

Bowlers do not choose at random. A bowler follows a short ball with a full one when they think it will work: against a batter who looks uncomfortable, on a pitch with bounce, with a field set for it. The sequences we observe were selected by someone with information we do not have. A raw comparison measures the bowler’s judgment along with the sequence.

The match situation changes everything. A batter in the last over of a Twenty20 innings swings at nearly every ball. The same batter at the start of an innings does not. The mix of deliveries also changes with the situation. Unless the situation is accounted for, an apparent effect of sequence can be an effect of the over number.

Batters adjust. If a particular sequence worked reliably, batters would learn to expect it, and it would stop working. So any effect that survives in the data is likely to be small, and small effects need many balls to detect.

The sequences multiply. With even a handful of delivery types, the number of two-ball and three-ball sequences grows quickly, and the number of balls behind each one shrinks. Estimates for rare sequences are mostly noise, the same problem I wrote about in the post on batting averages.

What a careful answer needs

A convincing analysis has to compare like with like: the same kind of batter, the same phase of the innings, the same kind of bowler, with only the previous delivery differing. It has to say how large an effect the data could have detected, so that “no effect found” is not confused with “no effect”. And it has to turn the estimate into something a bowler can use, which is a statement about what to bowl next and how much it is worth.

That last step matters most. An order effect that exists but is worth a hundredth of a run per ball is of no use to a captain. One that changes the best choice for the next delivery is.

Measurement and decision problems in sport are part of my consulting practice.

item.title: Why the usual reliability number is wrong for counts
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
A great deal of what we measure is a count. Goals in a match, sixes in an innings, defects in a batch, falls on a ward. When someone asks whether such a number is a reliable measure of the player, the line, or the ward, the usual answer is an intraclass correlation taken from a mixed model. For counts, that answer is often too high, and sometimes far too high.

Two scales, two questions

A count model works on two scales. On the log scale, the model says each player has an underlying rate. On the response scale, we see the counts themselves: 0, 1, 3, 0, 2.

The coefficient that software reports is usually computed on the log scale. It asks how much of the variation in underlying rates is between players. That is a fair question, but nobody ranks players on underlying rates. We rank them on the counts we observed, and the counts carry an extra layer of noise that the log scale leaves out: a batter with a steady rate of half a six per innings still hits none in most innings and two in a few.

A worked example

Suppose batters differ in their six-hitting rate, with an average of 0.5 sixes per innings and a between-batter standard deviation of 0.25. Suppose also that the rate is the only thing that differs between batters, so the log-scale coefficient is as high as it can be.

For a count with a given rate, the noise variance equals the rate. So for one innings:

  • between-batter variance of the rate: 0.25² = 0.0625
  • average counting noise: 0.5
  • reliability of one innings on the response scale: 0.0625 / (0.0625 + 0.5) = 0.11

A coefficient near 1 on one scale, and 0.11 on the scale where the ranking is done. Averaging over innings helps in the usual way: to reach a reliability of 0.8 for the average, this batter pool needs 32 innings. The numbers here are illustrative, chosen to make the arithmetic easy to check. The gap between the two scales is the point.

Zeros make it harder

Many counts have more zeros than a simple count model allows. Most innings contain no six at all, and whether a batter hits any is a partly separate matter from how many he hits once he starts. A hurdle model handles this with two parts, one for clearing zero and one for the size of the count after that. A reliability coefficient then has to combine both parts on the response scale, and the classical formulas do not say how.

That is the problem I took up in a paper in the Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics (2026), Response-scale reliability for count measurements, which works out the coefficient for hurdle models and applies it to six-hitting in Twenty20 cricket. The methods are in the dgt R package.

What to do with this

If your measure is a count and someone hands you a reliability coefficient, ask which scale it was computed on. If the answer is the model’s scale, treat it as an upper limit. Then ask how many observations sit under each number being compared. For rare events, the honest answer is usually “not enough yet”.

Measurement reliability for counts, proportions, and other non-normal data is part of my consulting practice.

item.title: How many judgments does an LLM-as-judge score need?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Many teams now score AI outputs with another model. The judge reads a response, applies a rubric, and returns a number. It is fast and cheap, and it has a problem that anyone who has run it twice has noticed: the score changes.

Run the same judge on the same response again and you may get a 7 instead of an 8. Swap in a different judge model and the scores shift again. So how many judgments should go into a score before you trust it? Measurement theory has had a direct answer to this question since the 1970s. It is called a decision study, and it comes from generalizability theory.

Where the variation comes from

Suppose you score a set of responses, and each response is judged several times. The judgments could be repeated runs of one judge, or runs of several different judges. An observed score then has three sources of variation:

  1. The responses. Some responses really are better than others. This is the variation you want to measure.
  2. The judge runs. Some runs, or some judges, are harsher than others across the board.
  3. Everything else. A run that likes one response and not another, plus plain noise.

Generalizability theory estimates how large each source is. These are variance components, and they come from an ordinary random-effects model fitted to the scores.

A worked example

Suppose the variance components come out as follows, as shares of the total variation in single judgments. The numbers are illustrative, not from any particular system.

Source Share of variance
Responses 0.40
Judge runs 0.10
Everything else 0.50

A single judgment, then, is mostly noise. Only 40% of the variation in one score reflects real differences between responses.

Averaging over several judgments shrinks the noise, and the decision study says by how much. There are two versions of the answer, depending on what the score is for.

  • For ranking responses against each other, only the third source matters, because a harsh run lowers every response equally. The reliability of an average of judgments is .
  • For comparing a score with a fixed bar, such as “ship if the mean is above 7”, the second source matters too, because a harsh run moves the score relative to the bar. The reliability is .
Judgments per response Reliability for ranking Reliability against a fixed bar
1 0.44 0.40
2 0.62 0.57
3 0.71 0.67
5 0.80 0.77
10 0.89 0.87

A common target is 0.80. Here that takes 5 judgments per response for ranking and 6 for a fixed bar. Reaching 0.90 takes 12 and 14. One judgment per response, which is how many pipelines run, gives a reliability below 0.5.

What this changes in practice

Measure before you decide. The variance components differ between tasks, rubrics, and judges. Score a sample of 50 to 100 responses with two or three judgments each, estimate the components, and then choose the number of judgments for the full run.

Several judges can beat one judge run several times. If one judge has a consistent bias, repeating it does not remove the bias. The decision study can compare “three runs of one judge” with “one run each of three judges” once both are in the pilot data.

More items usually beat more judgments. When the goal is to compare two systems rather than to score single responses, the number of test items often matters more than the number of judge runs. The same framework adds items as a source of variation and shows where the next unit of budget does the most good.

Report the reliability with the score. A benchmark score without a reliability is a measurement without its error bar.

Fitting the model

The variance components come from a random-effects model. In R, with one row per judgment, it is a few lines:

library(lme4)
fit <- lmer(score ~ 1 + (1 | response) + (1 | judge_run), data = scores)
VarCorr(fit)

The three variances printed are the response, judge-run, and residual components in the table above. Scores on a short ordinal scale, such as 1 to 5, can need a model for ordered categories instead, but the logic of the decision study is the same.

References

Cronbach, L. J., Gleser, G. C., Nanda, H., and Rajaratnam, N. (1972). The Dependability of Behavioral Measurements: Theory of Generalizability for Scores and Profiles. Wiley.

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability Theory. Springer.

Evaluation design and the reliability of rating pipelines are part of my consulting practice. See also Your leaderboard gap is probably noise.

item.title: What can a Combine tell you about Sundays?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Every spring, NFL teams gather the year’s draft prospects and time them. A player runs forty yards in shorts, alone, on a clean surface, and the result follows him for the rest of his career. Then he is drafted, and what matters is what he does in pads, on grass, with a three-hundred-pound opponent in the way.

This year’s NFL Big Data Bowl asks entrants to connect the two: tracking data from the Combine on one side, and what the same players did in regular-season games on the other. I entered, and my entry looks at defensive linemen. The results will wait until the competition closes in January. The question is worth a post now, because it is a measurement problem before it is a football problem.

Three reasons the link is hard to measure

The players you can check are not the players you measured. Hundreds of prospects run at the Combine. Game data exist only for those who were drafted, made a roster, and played. Teams choose those players partly on the Combine numbers themselves. So the group with both measurements has already been filtered on one of them, and any relationship seen in that group is weaker than the one in the full pool. A scout who concludes that a drill “does not predict much” may be looking at the filter and not at the drill.

One trial is a noisy reading. A prospect runs a drill once or twice. A start can be a few hundredths early or late for reasons that have nothing to do with ability. Before asking whether a Combine number predicts game performance, it is fair to ask how well it would predict itself on a second day. If the answer is “moderately”, then no game outcome can be predicted better than that.

The same word names two different events. A “first step” at the Combine is a reaction to the player’s own decision to go. A first step in a game is a reaction to the snap, taken from a stance chosen for the play, against a blocker who is also moving. Both can be clocked, and both are called get-off. Whether they measure the same quality is the thing to be shown, not assumed.

What a useful answer looks like

A front office does not need a correlation. It needs to know, for a given position, how much a tenth of a second at the Combine is worth in the games, and how sure anyone can be about that figure. An answer with honest uncertainty attached is more useful than a sharper one that falls apart when the next draft class arrives. It should also say where it does not apply. A result for defensive linemen says little about receivers.

That is the standard I have tried to hold the entry to. I will write about what it found after the January deadline.

Measurement problems of this kind, where the number in hand is a noisy stand-in for the thing you care about, are a large part of my consulting practice.

item.title: Writing a statistics paper that someone can use
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Most advice on academic writing is about sentences. The advice that has helped me most is about decisions made before the first sentence: who the paper is for, what it claims, and where it should go.

The best short guide I know on those decisions is Tim Swartz’s “Where Should I Publish My Sports Paper?” (The American Statistician, 2020). It is written for sports statistics, but most of it applies to any applied statistics paper. This post sets out what I took from it, followed by the habits I have added.

What I took from the guide

A good applied paper does two things. It has something new in the statistics, and it addresses a real problem in the application. The two pull against each other. A paper written to impress statisticians tends to treat the application as an afterthought, and a paper written for practitioners can have little in it that is new. The guide’s point is that the best papers manage both, and that an author should know which of the two a given paper is stronger on.

Practitioners adopt what they can follow. A method that works but cannot be explained to the people who would use it will not be used. The guide’s examples are methods that reached practice because the idea behind them could be stated plainly. I now ask of every method section whether a coach, a clinician, or an engineer could say in two sentences what the method does.

Choose the audience, then the journal. The same piece of work can be written for a statistics journal, an operations research journal, or a journal in the applied field. Each wants a different paper. Statistics journals want a substantial statistical contribution. Operations research journals value a solved problem. Journals in the applied field care most about what changes in practice. Choosing the audience first decides what goes in the introduction, how much theory stays in the main text, and what counts as the result.

Expect hard reviews and keep going. The guide is frank that reviewers question the assumptions in applied work closely, and that a paper rejected quickly at one journal can be published at another after a long review. Its advice is a thick skin. A rejection is information about the fit between the paper and the journal as often as it is about the work.

Get the work to readers. Applied work is scattered across disciplines, and a paper in the wrong place may never reach the people who could use it. The guide closes on a simple instruction: do good work and get it out.

What I have added

These are my own habits. They are not from the guide.

  1. Keep data, methods, results, and discussion apart. A reader who wants to know what was measured should not have to read the results to find out. When interpretation creeps into the methods section, I move it.
  2. Lead each result with what it means. The sentence a reader remembers should come first, and the number that supports it second.
  3. Give every number a comparison. A coefficient of 0.61 means little alone. Against a threshold, a previous study, or a second condition, it means something.
  4. Let tables carry the numbers and the text carry the pattern. A paragraph that repeats a table adds length without adding anything.
  5. State limitations with numbers. “The sample is small” is a hedge. “The estimate is based on 14 matches and would need about 40 to reach the usual standard” is a limitation the reader can weigh.
  6. Check every reference against the source. Author, year, volume, and pages, each one. A wrong citation is a small error that costs a large amount of trust.
  7. Write plainly. Short declarative sentences, no warm-up paragraphs, and no claim softened below what the evidence supports.

Why this matters outside journals

Everything above applies to a consulting report as much as to a paper. A client is a practitioner who has to act on the result. If they cannot follow what was done, cannot find the number they need, or cannot tell how far to trust it, the analysis has not done its job, however good the statistics are.

Reference. Swartz, T. B. (2020). Where should I publish my sports paper? The American Statistician 74(2), 103–108.

Clear reporting for the audience that has to use it is part of every engagement in my consulting practice.

item.title: Does the room change the speech?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Here’s a question about campaigns that sounds political but is really a measurement problem: when a candidate speaks in a deeply partisan state versus a competitive one, is it the same speech?

Political scientists have long theorized audience design — speakers tuning register to the room — but testing it at scale requires something that didn’t exist until recently: a way to score every campaign speech, not just the ones expert coders got to. Expert-coded populism databases are the field’s measurement standard, but they cover only eventual chief executives, which makes within-campaign questions unanswerable by design. My research program built a rubric-based large-language-model instrument for exactly this gap, validated against the Global Populism Database’s own coded speeches — including a held-out set of leaders never used during development — and stress-tested for the failure mode that matters most in campaign text: conflating ordinary adversarial campaigning with populism. With identity cues masked, the scores don’t move.

What the speeches show

Point that instrument at U.S. presidential campaign speeches from 2015 through 2024, record where each was delivered, and a pattern emerges.

For the Trump campaigns of 2016 and 2020 — where rally schedules provide the density of geographically distributed speeches the question needs — populist rhetoric intensifies with the partisanship of the rally’s state. The association survives the test that usually kills fragile campaign findings: a wild cluster bootstrap with states as clusters and the null imposed gives p = .0029. Decomposing the register shows the gradient is carried almost entirely by anti-elite language — a coefficient of about 4.5 anti-elite terms per thousand words (SE 1.7) along the state-partisanship scale — rather than by people-centric appeals. And the timing matters: a negative, statistically significant interaction (−1.16) shows the differentiation is strongest early in the campaign and saturates late, consistent with a candidate finding the register early and converging on it everywhere by the close.

Three checks discipline the interpretation. First, what kind of room matters: across a 32-specification curve, the state-partisanship effect is positive in every specification, while educational composition is significant in none — and racial-composition measures (white share, white non-college share) are similarly null. The audience feature the rhetoric tracks is partisanship, not demographics. Second, this is not a one-party artifact of range: Democratic candidates’ speech-to-speech variability (standard deviations of roughly .08–.13 on the populism scale) sits in the same neighbourhood as Trump’s (.11–.14), so the instrument could have detected the same tuning elsewhere; the strong gradient is where it is. Third, the honest null: pooled across six election cycles, the association is not statistically significant (p = .30) — the audience-design signal is a finding about specific campaigns with dense, geographically varied schedules, not a law of American politics. Reporting that null is not a weakness of the study; it is the study working.

Why a statistician cares

Strip the politics away and this is a chain of measurement problems: an instrument validated against a human-expert benchmark; a genre-specific calibration failure found and repaired; a generalizability study answering how many speeches and how many models a dependable score needs; and inference that respects the clustering in the data rather than pretending a few hundred speeches are a few hundred independent draws. The subject matter is rhetoric; the machinery is the same one I use on cricket averages and AI leaderboards. Whether a number can be trusted — and how much data that trust requires — is the same question everywhere.

Measurement with large language models — validation, calibration, and reliability — is part of my research program and consulting practice.

item.title: How many innings before a batting average means anything?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Every cricket argument eventually reaches for an average. A newcomer has 142 runs from four T20 innings and the selection debate treats the number as evidence. A veteran has two lean series and the same arithmetic becomes a case for dropping him. The question nobody asks of the number itself: at this sample size, is it measuring the batter — or the weather of four particular days?

Batting is a noisy instrument

The same batter, in the same form, against comparable attacks, can score 3 on Tuesday and 78 on Saturday without anything about the batter changing. Dismissal is abrupt and partly circumstantial; one ball ends the observation. So a single innings is an extremely noisy reading of ability, and the interesting question becomes quantitative: how much of the innings-to-innings variation in scores reflects real differences between batters, and how much is occasion noise?

That’s a measurement-theory question, and generalizability theory answers it by decomposing the variance: a between-batter component (signal) and a within-batter component (everything the batter doesn’t control twice). I first estimated these components for T20 batting in a 2014 conference paper with colleagues at the Institute of Applied Statistics, Sri Lanka, applying random-effects ANOVA through a generalizability lens — the seed of a research program I’m still working on. The recurring finding, in cricket as in every sport I’ve since studied: the signal share of a single observation is small. Ability differences are real, but any one innings is mostly noise.

The arithmetic of patience

Averages fix this — slowly. The reliability of a k-innings average follows the Spearman–Brown relationship: it climbs with k, but with hard diminishing returns. Suppose, illustratively, that batter skill accounts for 10% of the variance in a single innings score. Then reaching even a moderate reliability of 0.7 for the average takes 21 innings; reaching 0.8 takes 36. If the single-innings signal share is 5%, those numbers become 45 and 76. In T20, where a specialist bats perhaps 15–25 innings in a year, that’s a season or more before the average deserves the trust routinely placed in it — and a three-match trial is, statistically, close to a coin flip wearing a scorecard.

This is the same lesson as team shooting indicators in handball and AI leaderboards, which is exactly the point: a batting average, a shooting percentage, and an Elo rating are all measurement instruments, and instruments have reliability that depends on how many observations they aggregate. The domain changes; the arithmetic doesn’t.

Two honest complications

First, cricket scores are not tidy bell-curve data — they’re zero-heavy, right-skewed, and censored by not-outs — and that structure genuinely complicates reliability arithmetic; extending the classical machinery to handle count data of this kind is the subject of a paper of mine in the Australian & New Zealand Journal of Statistics (2026), which applies it to six-hitting in Twenty20 cricket. Second, none of this says small samples carry no information: a Bayesian selector shades priors on four innings, sensibly. What the reliability lens forbids is the stronger, everyday claim — treating a small-sample average as a ranking of ability. At those sample sizes, the ranking is mostly re-ordering noise.

The practical upshot for anyone who selects, trades, or argues about players: ask how many observations sit under a number before asking what the number says. Patience isn’t just a virtue in cricket — it’s a sample-size requirement.

Measurement reliability — how many observations a trustworthy number needs — is a core thread of my research and consulting practice, in sport and well beyond it.

item.title: Testing one thing at a time is costing you
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Picture a team tuning a process — a reactor, a coating line, a recipe, a web page. Three settings might matter: temperature, time, concentration. The careful-sounding plan: hold everything constant, change temperature, observe. Reset, change time, observe. Reset, change concentration, observe. One factor at a time, so you “know what caused what.”

It feels rigorous. It’s actually the expensive way to learn less. This has been known since R. A. Fisher was designing agricultural experiments in the 1920s, and it still surprises people every time the arithmetic is laid out.

The same eight runs, spent two ways

Give both strategies an identical budget: eight experimental runs, three factors, each at two levels (low/high).

One-factor-at-a-time (OFAT): four distinct conditions — a baseline plus one change per factor — run twice each to get some replication. Each factor’s effect is estimated by comparing two runs against two runs. Four of the eight runs sit in the baseline doing bookkeeping.

Factorial: run all combinations once. Here’s the part that looks like an accounting trick and isn’t: every run participates in every estimate. The temperature effect is the average of the four high-temperature runs minus the average of the four low-temperature runs — and the same eight runs, regrouped, estimate the time effect and the concentration effect too. Statisticians call it hidden replication.

The consequence is quantifiable: with the same eight runs, the factorial’s effect estimates have half the variance of the OFAT estimates. Same budget, twice the precision, on every factor at once — and the gap widens as factors are added.

The bigger problem: interactions

Precision is the smaller half of the argument. OFAT’s structural flaw is that it cannot see interactions — cases where the effect of one factor depends on the level of another. Suppose higher temperature helps at short times but hurts at long ones. OFAT tested temperature only at the baseline time, found “temperature helps,” and locked in a conclusion that’s wrong across half the operating range. Worse, OFAT’s endpoint depends on the path: change the factors in a different order and you can walk to a different “optimum,” because each step is conditioned on wherever the previous steps left you.

The factorial estimates the interactions from the same eight runs — no extra budget. In real processes, interactions aren’t the exception; they’re routinely where the actual optimum hides.

“But I have ten factors”

The objection writes itself: is 1,024 runs. This is precisely what fractional factorial designs are for — carefully chosen subsets that screen many factors in few runs. Seven factors in eight runs is a standard screening design; the price is that some effects share estimates (aliasing), and the craft is choosing a fraction whose ambiguities fall on effects you’re prepared to assume away. Sorting the handful of factors that matter from the many that don’t is usually the highest-value experiment a team ever runs — then a focused follow-up study optimizes the survivors.

The through-line: the runs are the expensive part, whether each one is a day of reactor time or a week of user traffic. Design is how you make each run answer several questions at once.

Designing experiments — factorial, fractional-factorial, and screening studies for product, process, and lab work — is a core part of my consulting practice. The best time to involve a statistician is before the first run.

item.title: How many participants do you actually need?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
It’s the most common question a statistician gets, usually asked as if it had a universal answer: how many participants do I need? Thirty? A hundred? Whatever the last paper in your field used?

The honest answer is that “how many” is the last step of a calculation, not the first. The first step is a question only you can answer: what is the smallest effect that would still matter?

The logic, in one paragraph

A study is a measuring instrument, and sample size sets its resolution. If a real effect exists, a bigger sample makes you more likely to detect it; the probability of detecting it is the study’s power. Powering a study means choosing the effect size you refuse to miss, then buying enough data to see it. Choose that effect honestly — the smallest difference that would change a decision, a treatment, a design — and the arithmetic follows. Choose it by working backwards from the sample you can afford, and the arithmetic will happily launder your budget into a number that looks scientific.

A rule of thumb worth knowing

For the simplest case — comparing two groups on a continuous outcome, aiming for the conventional 80% power at the 5% significance level — there’s a remarkably compact approximation:

where is the effect size in standard-deviation units. Run the numbers and the stakes become vivid. A large effect () needs about 25 per group — 50 people. A medium effect () needs about 63 per group — 126 people. A small effect () needs nearly 400 per group — close to 800 in total.

That last line is the one that changes plans. Small effects are common in real research, and the difference between “we can see medium effects” and “we can see small effects” is not a modest top-up — it’s a sixfold larger study. Better to know that before the ethics application than after the data disappoint.

Real designs complicate the arithmetic in both directions: repeated measures and paired designs buy power cheaply; clustered data (patients within clinics, students within classrooms) quietly costs it, sometimes severely; and dropout means recruiting more than the calculation says. None of that changes the logic — it changes the inputs.

Two things reviewers notice

A justified effect size. Grant panels have seen a thousand power sections that assume a “medium effect” because the template did. What earns credibility is an effect size argued from something — a pilot study, prior literature, a minimal clinically important difference — with the power statement built on it.

No post-hoc power. If a study comes back non-significant, computing “the power we had, given the effect we observed” adds nothing: observed power is just the p-value in a costume, and a low value re-states the non-significance it pretends to explain. The time for power analysis is before the data exist. Afterwards, the informative quantity is the confidence interval — it shows what effect sizes your study could and couldn’t rule out.

The order of operations

Decide what effect matters and defend the number. Estimate the variability from a pilot or the literature. Account for the design — pairing, clustering, dropout. Then compute n. If the answer is unaffordable, the honest moves are to change the design, sharpen the measurement, or study a bigger effect — not to quietly relax the power.

Sample-size justification, power analysis, and statistical-analysis plans for grant applications are part of my consulting practice — and the design stage is exactly the right time to talk.

item.title: Your leaderboard gap is probably noise
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Somewhere right now, a team is choosing which AI model to build on because it sits one place higher on a leaderboard. The gap might be two points of win rate, or a handful of Elo. Here’s the uncomfortable question a statistician has to ask: is that gap a fact about the models, or a fact about the sample?

A two-minute calculation

Suppose model A beats model B in 62% of head-to-head comparisons, and model B wins 60% of its own matchups, each measured over 500 votes. Two points apart — feels decisive on a ranking table.

The standard error of a proportion around 0.6 on 500 votes is — about 2.2 percentage points per model. The uncertainty on the difference between them is larger still, roughly points. A 2-point observed gap against ~3 points of noise, before any multiple-comparison correction, isn’t evidence of a real difference. It’s a tie wearing a trophy.

This isn’t a contrived example. Public arena leaderboards now publish confidence intervals precisely because the intervals at the top routinely overlap — the rank order among the leading models is partly an artifact of sampling. And the problem compounds: with ten models, there are forty-five pairwise comparisons, so a few “significant-looking” gaps will appear by chance even if nothing real separates anyone.

The deeper problem: rankings are measurements

A leaderboard is a measurement instrument, and instruments have reliability. The question that matters isn’t only “is this gap significant today?” but “if we collected the same number of votes again, would the ranking come back the same?” Those are different questions. A gap can clear a significance test while the ranking built from many such gaps remains unstable — flip a few hundred votes and third place becomes sixth.

Measurement theory has a name for this and a toolbox for it: you decompose the variation in observed scores into the part that reflects real differences between the things being ranked and the part that’s occasion-to-occasion noise, then compute how many observations you’d need before the ranking is dependable at the level you care about. The recurring finding, in domain after domain, is that the number is larger than people expect — often much larger than the data anyone has.

How to read a leaderboard without fooling yourself

Ask for the interval, not the point: if the intervals of two entries overlap, treat them as tied, whatever the rank order says. Ask for the n behind each comparison — a rating built on 80 matchups and one built on 8,000 do not deserve the same trust. Be most suspicious exactly where the stakes feel highest, at the top, where entries are closest and gaps are smallest relative to noise. And if a decision genuinely hangs on the comparison — which model to license, which system to ship — run your own evaluation on your own task distribution, sized in advance so the answer will be reliable. That last step is a sample-size calculation, and it’s cheaper than choosing the wrong model.

None of this is exotic statistics. It’s the same discipline clinical trials have used for decades, pointed at a new kind of scoreboard. The scoreboards are new; the arithmetic isn’t.

I consult on exactly these questions — evaluation design, the reliability of ranking and judging pipelines, and how much data a trustworthy verdict needs. If your team is making decisions off a leaderboard, let’s talk.

item.title: Building this site: Quarto, GitHub Pages, and a win-probability worm
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
I wanted a single place to publish my work: my consulting practice, the interactive tools I build, and writeups of the research behind them. A few constraints made the choice easy.

Everything I do already lives in R and LaTeX. I’m deepening Git this sabbatical, so a plain-text site under version control is a feature, not a chore. And I didn’t want a monthly bill for a CMS I’d have to wrestle. Quarto on GitHub Pages ticks all three: posts are .qmd files, the whole site is a git repository I own, and hosting is free.

The worm

The graphic on the projects page is a win-probability worm — the line that swings across the 50% mark as a chase unfolds. On the site it’s a lightweight SVG widget: between matches it replays recent internationals from precomputed model output, and during a live game it updates as the match unfolds.

What’s next

More tools are on the way — tennis and soccer forecasters are in final development — along with methodology posts on how to design studies and trust measurements.

More soon.

item.title: How many observations before a statistic means anything?
item.dc:creator: Ruwan C. Karunanayaka
item.description:
Coaches, analysts, and managers rank people on performance indicators — shooting percentage, conversion rate, error rate — often after only a handful of observations. The uncomfortable question is whether those numbers reflect the person or just the occasion.

The framing

This is a measurement problem, and generalizability theory is built for it. A G-study decomposes the variance in an indicator into the part attributable to the thing you care about (the signal) and the parts attributable to occasion-to-occasion fluctuation and residual noise. A decision study then answers the practical question directly: how many observations do you need before the indicator dependably separates one performer from another?

The answers are frequently sobering. Across the sports settings I’ve studied, indicators differ sharply in how quickly they stabilize — some are trustworthy within a handful of games, while others need more observations than a season typically provides before the ranking they imply means anything.

Why it matters

If a metric needs fifteen matches to be reliable and you’re acting on three, you’re ranking noise. The value of the decision-study table is that it tells you, per indicator, where that line sits — so you know which numbers to trust early and which to wait on. The same logic applies far beyond sport: clinical measures, quality-control metrics, student assessment.

The dgt R package implements these calculations.
